Stevens was named the Eastern Conference Coach of the Month for April 2015. He led the Celtics to the East's best record in April at 7–1. The Celtics recorded a 4–0 mark on the road, and closed the month with six consecutive victories—five of them against playoff teams.[[87]](#cite_note-87) On February 28, 2016, Stevens was named the Eastern Conference Coach of the Month for February. There have been various proposals to expand the G7. The U.S.-based Atlantic Council has held the [D-10 Strategy Forum](/wiki/D-10_Strategy_Forum "D-10 Strategy Forum") since 2014 with representatives from what it calls "leading democracies" which support a "rules-based democratic order", consisting of all members of the G7 (including the [European Union](/wiki/European_Union "European Union")) plus [Australia](/wiki/Australia "Australia") and [South Korea](/wiki/South_Korea "South Korea"). Several democratic countries – including [India](/wiki/India "India"), [Indonesia](/wiki/Indonesia "Indonesia"), [Poland](/wiki/Poland "Poland"), and [Spain](/wiki/Spain "Spain") – participate as observers.[[32]](#cite_note-auto1-32) Centered around a similar mandate as the G7, the D-10 has been considered by some analysts to be an alternative to the group;[[33]](#cite_note-:0-33) This is also favored by various [think tanks](/wiki/Think_tank "Think tank") and former [British leader Boris Johnson](/wiki/Boris_Johnson "Boris Johnson").[[32]](#cite_note-auto1-32)

In 2019 under [Putin](/wiki/Vladimir_Putin "Vladimir Putin"), [Russia](/wiki/Russia "Russia") had signaled support for the inclusion of [China](/wiki/China "China"), India, and [Turkey](/wiki/Turkey "Turkey") if the G7 had reinstated Russian membership.[[34]](#cite_note-34)

In 2020 under [Trump](/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump"), the U.S. had signaled support for the inclusion of Australia, [Brazil](/wiki/Brazil "Brazil"), India, and South Korea, plus the reincorporation of Russia.[[35]](#cite_note-35)[[36]](#cite_note-36) The leaders of the other six G7 members unanimously rejected this proposal.[[37]](#cite_note-37)

Also in November 2020, [Jared Cohen](/wiki/Jared_Cohen "Jared Cohen") and [Richard Fontaine](/wiki/Richard_Fontaine "Richard Fontaine"), writing in *[Foreign Affairs](/wiki/Foreign_Affairs "Foreign Affairs")*, suggested that the G7 might be expanded

United Nations Security Council :: Reform :: G4 proposal :: chunk_0028
The [G4 nations](/wiki/G4_nations "G4 nations") (Brazil, Germany, India, and Japan) have campaigned for permanent seats on the Security Council, arguing that the body's composition reflects the geopolitical realities of 1945 rather than the contemporary world. Their core proposal calls for expanding the Council from 15 to 25 or 26 members, with six new permanent seats –two for Africa, two for the Asia-Pacific, one for Latin America and the Caribbean, and one for Western Europe and Others –though the new permanent members would not immediately gain veto power, with the question to be reviewed after a transition period of 10 to 15 years.[[154]](#cite_note-158) Japan and Germany had been the UN's second- and third-largest funders, respectively, before China took over as the second largest funder in recent years, whilst Brazil and India are two of the largest contributors of troops to UN-mandated peacekeeping missions.

In 2017, the G4 nations indicated willingness temporarily to forgo [veto power](/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_veto_power "United Nations Security Council veto power") if granted [permanent seats](/wiki/Permanent_members_of_the_United_Nations_Security_Council "Permanent members of the United Nations Security Council").[[155]](#cite_note-159)

The permanent members have announced their positions on Security Council reform reluctantly. The United States has supported the permanent membership of Japan and lent its support to India and a small number of additional non-permanent members. The United Kingdom and France have essentially supported the G4 position, with the expansion of permanent and non-permanent members and the accession of Germany, Brazil, India, and Japan to permanent member status, as well as an increase in the presence of African countries on the Council. China has supported stronger representation of developing countries and has firmly opposed Japan's membership.[

On the [review aggregator](/wiki/Review_aggregator "Review aggregator") website [Rotten Tomatoes](/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), 99% of 87 critics' reviews are positive, with an average rating of 8.3/10. The website's consensus reads: "A poetic tribute to tenacity, *All That Breathes* uses two brothers' tireless efforts to make a broader point about finding triumph within tragedy."[[26]](#cite_note-26) [Metacritic](/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), which uses a [weighted average](/wiki/Weighted_arithmetic_mean "Weighted arithmetic mean"), assigned the film a score of 87 out of 100, based on 19 critics, indicating "universal acclaim".[[27]](#cite_note-27)

Daniel Fienberg of *[The Hollywood Reporter](/wiki/The_Hollywood_Reporter "The Hollywood Reporter")*, reviewing the film wrote, "Sen has encapsulated a vision of New Delhi in which modern life, particularly pollution and overpopulation, have placed new strain on the balance between humans and nature." Praising the film he further stated that the film "is one of the more dreamily provocative documentaries I’ve ever seen." Fienberg concluding his review remarked, "In this tiny marvel of a documentary, it’s a little and a lot all at once".[[28]](#cite_note-28)
Dennis Harvey reviewing for *[Variety](/wiki/Variety_(magazine) "Variety (magazine)")* praised the score of the film, writing, "The meditative yet ingratiating impact is furthered by Roger Goula’s score, which strikes aptly spectral notes." He also appreciated the cinematography and wrote, "There’s an inventive lyricism to the imagery here, aesthetically unified despite three credited cinematographers." Concluding his review Harvey stated, "With a tone more melancholic and charming than one might expect given the various crises at play here, Sen's deceptively casual observational documentary prefers dwelling on resistance and resilience to pronouncements of doom."[[29]](#cite_note-29) Josh Flanders
